summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. In respect of certain items of assets belonging to the assessee on the basis of which he claimed that it had been sold in the previous year, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1, 50, 000 estimated as the accrued interest on the amount of the assessee's money lending investments. The Wealth Tax officer disallowed the claim of the asses see. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the additions of Rs., 1, 00, 000 and allowed the appeals filed by the assessee. The Revenue appealed to the Appellate Tribunal and contended that the expression " net wealth " is not defined in the Income Tax Act, 1922 as the value of a property cannot be determined under the Income tax Act, 1961. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the view taken by the Orissa High Court in Ved rev a Venk appa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, West Bengal, [ 1960 ] Supp. 2 S. C. R. 10 48, approved.

The respondent was a public servant. He was charged with the following acts of misconduct: (1) he had committed an act of misconduct and prepared his pay roll for the month of May 1969, which resulted in the charge of and the respondent was convicted by the competent authority under r. 3 of the Indian Civil Service Servants (Disciplinary & Appeal) Rules, 1966. The respondent challenged the findings of the Inquiry Officer before the High Court. The High Court held that the penalty imposed on him was disproportionate to the proved charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the punishment awarded to him was harsh and disproportionate to his misconduct and that the Tribunal erred in holding that the respondent had been guilty of the charge framed against him. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has no power to interfere with the finding of the disciplinary au thor ity. [ 10 E F ] 2. The disciplinary authority must, however, bear in mind the nature of the criminal case, the Trib un al may be a nd the penalty be adequate. It is not necessary that the delinquent should be given a reasonable opportunity to defend himself. If the penalty is imposed on the basis of conviction by a criminal court, the Tribunal may examine the adequacy of the penalty inflicted in the light of the con di tion and sentence imposed on such officer. But if the penal ty impugned is manifestly unreasonable or unfair, the order of the Governor on whose powers it wi ll be quashed with liberty to hold fresh enquiry. [ 11 G H; 12 A B ] 3. The penalty imposed upon the respondent is commensurate to the gravity of mis de mean our established. The punishment imposed can be sustained from the date of the order. [ 13 D E ] 4. The principles of natural justice are not rigid rules but are flex ible. The doctrine of proportionality is not a rule of law but is a rule made by the State Government. The burden of proof is heavy on the shoul ders of the delinquent. The delinquent employee has not been able to prove any of the charges. The Trib un ary has not discharged the burden of proving the guilt of the public servant, but has to establish that the charges are so grave that no loss to the Government for the man w ho led. [ 14 C D ] 5. The strict rules of evidence and the procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure do not apply to departmental proceedings and the rules have to be strictly followed. The standard of proof of the offence is one of preponderance of probability. The preponderance of probabilities is the foundation of the prosecution. There could be accepted no evidence. The delinqu ency is a matter of inference. The onus of proof lies on the delinquent employee. The prosecution has to prove the charge beyond a shadow of doubt. [ 15 E F ].

The appellant, a tenant in respect of certain premises, was the lessee in respect thereof. He had paid rent upto the end of December 1967 and the first installment of 1968 but the landlord did not pay the same till the end. The appellant filed an application under section 7 (1) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1964 for restoration of possession on the ground that he was the lawful tenant of the premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was no more than the landlord who had been evicted from the premises by the defendant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata since the tenancy stood terminated by efflux of time and the plaintiff could not be dispossessed without the leave of the court. Held: (i) The High Court erred in holding that there was no bar against the grant of leave to the appellant to file an appeal against the dismissal order. (ii) The provisions of section 7 of the Act were applicable only to cases where the Civil Court has jurisdiction to decide questions such as: (a) whether any person is a tenant or a protected tenant; (b) if he is a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Rent Act, the Mamlatdar shall after holding an enquiry determine the question whether a person is tenant or not; and (c) the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar under the statute.

The petitioners were engaged in the construction industry. They were given all benefits due to them under the various labour legislations. In the year 1985, they were treated as'daily rated employees'and were paid a sti pend by the Corporation. On the basis of the recommendations of the Committee constituted under the Act, they claimed payment of wages at the rate of Rs. 1, 000 per month. The Corporation contended that the work was not superv ised by the State Government but the State had adopted the minimum wages payable to the workmen. The Court held that the Corporation was entitled to fix the pay scale of the workmen at the same time. The petitioners filed an application before the Labour Commissioner for enforcement of their fundamental right to " equal pay for equal work ". The Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners were entitled to the pay scales of the regular employees. The petitioner challenged the order of the Labour Court contending that the principle of " equal salary for equal pay " is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The doctrine of " Equal pay for Equal pay " cannot be invoked ordinarily in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It has been made clear that the differential treatment will be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or she lear ns also by experience as much as by other means. [ 669 B C ] (ii) The principle of equal pay is not a universal concept which requires a distinction between the two classes of employees. [ 670 F G ] (iii) The difference between the basic pay and the basic wage fixed for similar work is not merely a differenti ation between the different classes of workers. The standard of living and the standard of work performed can be different from the standard prescribed by the relevant rules. [ 671 E ] (iv) The question whether the petitioners are entitled to " just wages " is a matter of degree and it is not possible to determine if there is discrimination among the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment. [ 672 D ] (v) The equality claims of the petitioners could be allowed only when there is a discrimination amongst the same sets of employees in the present case. The prosecution case against accused 1 and 6 was that they had committed the murder of Mal an, daughter of A. P. W. 1 and his wife in respect of the murder. The Sessions Judge found them guilty of the charge under section 302 read with section 120B I. P., C. P.. C. Act and convicted them for the offence of murder under section 304 read with Section 34 I. p. I. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the conviction of A and B were not sustainable. Held, that the acquittal of A was not justified in law because it was a case of no evidence against A and A and that the High court erred in holding that the appellant alone was guilty of charge No. 2. The High Court rightly acquitted A and the sentence awarded to him.

The appellant, a son of the deceased, was married to one G. Par thas ar athy, who died in July 1945. He was married and by his wife, the appellant, who was the eld est daughter of G. Pun nam ma, died on September 26, 1945. On September 26,. 1945, the couple had three children, one of whom was aged about 5 years and the other of the appellant. In the suit for partition filed by G. P. I., the appellant claimed that G. Kal bag al's father was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 and that on her death G. R. I. was entitled to a share in item No. 1 and that G was not entitled to any share in the properties. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that G had no right to sell the property under the will and that the appellant was entitled for the entire amount of Rs. 10, 320 as gift with interest. Held: (i) that the High court was wrong in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the test at rix fully understood the nature of the recitals in the will. It is true that the evidence of the plaintiff was dis interested and so it could be accepted that he did not have the necessary ingredients of the document. But the fact that the plaintiff obtained a power of attorney from the test in question does not show satisfactorily that the Will was read out to the test. (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the testator was acting of his own free will in executing the will; and (iii) that even if the scribe had not been examined, the test would not be satisfied. (iv) that in recording these conclusions, the High Judge has mis directed himself in law because the evidence showed that the scribe was aware of the execution of the will before he was alive.

The appellants, who were manufacturers of motor vehicles, imported certain goods under entry No. 4 of the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, and claimed exemption from payment of tax on the ground that they fall within entry No 5 of the schedule to the Act. The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes allowed an application for producing their account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cin em as or for any other use. The Appellate Tribunal held that the goods fell within entry Nos. 4, 6 and 7 of the 1st Schedule to that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the entry in question did not cover the subject matter of entry No 4 of Schedule 1 of the Act, because the goods were not covered by entry No 2 of Schedule I of the said Act. Held: (i) that the entries in the schedule relate to motor vehicles and includes component parts thereof. The entry No 3 is not a general entry but only a secondary to the fact that the word access ory is used in the sched ules. The expression " accessories " is used to describe the goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. The term'accessories'is used for the purpose of being used in connection with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No 6 of Schedule II of the Madras General Sales tax Act, 1953, the expression occurs at the end as follows: " Photo graphic and other cam eras and substitute for use therein. " A tractor " is not an essential part of a type writer so as to attract the tax under entry 18 of the second schedule to that article. [ 562 B C ] (ii) The entry in the Schedule relates to motor vehicle and not to goods which are specifically mentioned in the entry No, 4. The words " parts thereof " are used in different terms in the context of Entry No. 5 of Schedule V of the Bombay Sales Tax. It is not possible to find out whether the articles are of a kind specified in the first schedule to be used in a particular type of type of motor vehicle.

The petitioners were licensees of minor minerals. They challenged the validity of the Act by filing petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution, contending that the State Government was empowered to levy royalty in respect of minor mineral and that the petitioners were not entitled to any concession in respect thereof. The petitioners contended that the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. The Act was passed in the year 1957 by Parliament to provide for the regulation of mines and development and conservation of minerals. The State Government enacted the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 which came into force on 1 7 1985. Rule 21 of the Rules provided that the lease shall be granted for one year ending 31st December of the year. The Rules further provided that no royalty shall be charged from the lessee except with the previous sanction of the President. The petitioner's case was that the provisions of the Bombay Minor Mineral (Valid ation) Act, 1958, which authorised the State Govern ment to levy the royalty in certain areas of lim estone, K ankar, Mur ram and Gra vel etc., were ultra vires the powers conferred on the State Legislature by section 15 of the. The question whether the Act was a law made by the State legislature or the State Legislatures was considered by this Court in the case of [ Indian Cement Ltd. vs The State of Tamil Nadu ];, followed. In the instant case the imposition of royalty in the State of Gujarat on the minor minerals was illegal as it did not contraven e the provisions Of article 301 of the constitution. The tax was imposed on the extracted mineral and the same could not be levied without the previous approval of the president. The impugned notification dated 26 6 1985 was issued by the Government of Gujarat exercising the power under section 15 (2) of the, and the said notification was valid ated by the Central Government. The deceased was a le per, who was sleeping on the eastern side of his house. He was sleeping in his courtyard and he saw two persons running ahead of him. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crow d gathered at the place where he was sleeping and when he was sitting, he found one person running away from the place of occurrence. He ran to his elder brother's house and went there. When he reached near the scene of occurrence he was already dead. His wife was also called by PW 4. On hearing the sh outs of PW 4, the police came to the spot and recorded the statement of PW 1 under section 161 Cr. P. C. The evidence of PW 2 was rejected by the Sessions Judge as usual and the accused was acquitted. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court should not have relied on the testimony of PW 3 because the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the testimony given by PW 2 is unreliable. [ 709 E ] (ii) There are more than one eye witness for the prosecution to prove the fact that the deceased tried to be strang ulated by the assailants. It is clear that the trial court has not considered the basic quality of the evidence of the witnesses. [ 710 G H; 711 A B ] (iii) The very fact that PW 4 had stated in the first information report that " my younger brother'(meaning the deceased) was " ch asing him from behind " in court he has completely given a go by to this statement and stated that Karun akar an was being chased by PWs 1, 2, and 3. [ 711 D F ] (iv) The evidence regarding the presence of PW 5 in the site plan does not inspire confidence since the witness may not have seen the other. There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the place plan. There were more than two witnesses out of that crow d produced in court for the purpose of contradict ing the PW 1.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business of solic itors. The income tax Officer, in the assessment year 1950 51, assessed the amounts in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives of Amar chand and imposed a penalty under section 24 B of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amount which was received by the heirs of Amar Chand as a Hindu undivided family was not taxable because the income from the business was liable to be taxed under section 23 (4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the expression " or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died " did not mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and heir and after his death, they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have continued. The word " or " in section 24 A means only such persons who were liable to pay tax out of their estate. The words " if he has not died ", are used in section 2 (1)( b) of that Act and therefore the word " shall " in the section means only those persons who are liable to paying tax out or whose property is capable of meeting the charge.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They were working in various offices located in the States of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969 they were working as such in different offices situated in the cities of Hyderabad, Hyderabad and Hyderabad. In the meanwhile, the Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification under section 3 (1) of the Public Employment (Require ment as to Res idence) Act, 1957 for domic iles of Tel eng ana region. The appellant was a post man in the Bulandsha hr Police Station. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in the trial he was convicted by the Additional Sessions judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had not found him guilty of the offence under section 53 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay fine. Held, that the conviction's and sentences passed against the appellant were liable to be set aside. It is sufficient to say that the appellant could have been convicted only with the aid of section 34 of the Penal Code. The appellant could not be said to have trans gressed the provisions of section 345 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecution has failed to prove that the articles were stolen or stolen from the possession of the accused. The evidence has been believed by the High court as well as by the Sessions Judge. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had established that the five registered letters in question were in the exclusive possession of appellant. The fact that the al mir ah contained some articles which were seized at the time of the raid was not proved. The mere fact that there were two letters in the post office would not make the appellant liable to the punishment of the charge under section 51 of the Post Office act. The first part of the argument that the two letters were not received by them was not correct. The second part of this contention was also rejected.

The appellant, a resident of the State of Uttar Pradesh, was elected as a member of the Panchayat. He filed an application under section 85 of the U. P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, to the High Court for quashing the order of the S. D. M., dated November 28, 1963, and on December 20, 1963 he was served with a notice to assem ble on December 25, 1963. On December 21, 1963 the S, D. A. made an application before the Ny aya Panchayat praying that the proceedings in the case be stayed pending receipt of the stay order. The S, I. O. who issued the order refused to take it on record. Thereupon the appellant moved an application for leave to appeal against the order passed by the Ny ay ati Panchayat. The High Court allowed the application and stayed further proceedings till December 26, 1963 and directed that the proceeding be stayed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to stay the proceedings before the Si ba Panchayat and that the order was not binding on him. Held: (i) The High court erred in holding that the Sarpanch and the Pan ch as had knowledge of the existence of the order. It was not correct to say that the so called affidavit was not sworn to before any person authorised to administer oath s. The fact that the appellant did not know about the filing of the application before him, was immaterial. The appellant's conduct in making an application was not bona fide and therefore could not be said to have been proved. (ii) The appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. (iii) The order of remand was not illegal because the appellant had not filed the proper affidavit in support of his allegations. (iv) The power of the High Courts to stay proceedings before a Ny aya panchayat is a serious matter and a High Court should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that there was no evidence at all. (v) The orders were not passed in accordance with law.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302, I. P. C., and sentenced to death. He filed a complaint against the appellant for the offence punishable under section 307, I.. P. c. and also for an offence under Section 302, IPC. The Sessions Judge acquitted him but convicted him of the charge under section 304, I,. P. Code, and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in rejecting his statement as being inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not proved. Held, that the conviction of the accused under section 303, I., P. P., C., is correct. It was not necessary to consider whether the facts which had been proved against the accused were sufficient to establish that the accused had committed the murder of Sheo Sahai.

The petitioners, who were the respondents in the writ petition before the High Court, challenged the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that they had not been issued a notice under Rule 4 (1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. They also prayed for the issue of an interim order staying the poll which had been fixed to be held on December 31, 1978. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions and directed the issue to be proceeded on merits. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed as there was no evidence in support of their claim and that the appellants were not informed about the defect in the notice. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the writ petitions were maintainable because the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High court, and the High Courts were justified in refusing to interfere with the election process. [ 10 E F ] (ii) The writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the validity and the election of the remaining 48 candidates were not barred by limitation. [ 11 G H; 12 B ] (iii) The appellants were entitled to the issue as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored.

The appellant company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to give information under section 220 (1) of the, which was punishable under section 135 (2). The High Court held that the company and their directors could not be convicted under section 138 (4) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words " were so read not strictly construed as having been used in sections 32 and 131 of the Companies Act or in section 130 of the Act did not apply to the case because the word " shall " in section 220 of the 1956 Act had a wide connotation. HELD: (i) The expression " may " in s. 221 of the Indian Penal Code means any person who is charged with an offence. [ 414 E ] (ii) The word " may ", in section 222 of the Code means every other person who has been charged with the offence. It is clear that the section does not say that the word'may'should be interpreted is the same way. The word'shall'in section 221 of that Code means only such persons who have been charged together with the amount of the cheque. [ 415 G H; 416 A B ] (iii) The section in the English Act is a composite one which lays down various requirements which are to be complied with even though they are not fulfilled. The section does n't prescribe any particular mode of payment. The provision under section 169 of the said Act is intended to cover all the cases where the principle laid down in the section is applicable.

The respondent was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three years under section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. He was convicted by a Single Judge of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. On appeal, the Division Bench held that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case because section 5 of the Act did not empower the State Government to direct the investigation into the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " any other offence " in section 5 is wide enough to include an individual case and that the word " person " used in section 3 must be read as " person accused of an offence ". Held: (i) that the words " any person subject to the provisions of the Code for the trial of warrant cases by the Magistrate " in sections 6 to 15 prescribe the special procedure which the court has to follow in deciding whether or not there is a prima facie case against a person charged with offences and that therefore the expression'person accused'in section 2 (1)( c) of that Act would include an " individual case ", and that section 5 does not apply to the case where the offence is committed by a person who is being tried at the commencement of the trial. (ii) that section 4 of the Calcutta Special Courts Act, 1950 off ends the provisions Of article 14 of the Con sti t ution of India Act, 1935, and is therefore ultra vires Article 14 of Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Radi ology in the Central Health Service on May 5, 1963. He was appointed to the post of Assistant Professor of Medical Medicine and was also required to be posted at the time scale of pay. In the year 1963 he was appointed in the senior scale. He joined the service under r. 8 (2A) of the Central Civil Services (Classification and Appeal) Rules, 1966. He continued to work as an Associate Professor in the Government Hospital till September 9, 1966 when he was promoted to the higher post. On July 1, 1963 he made a request for his promotion to the next higher post of Professor of Medic ines. The appellant's representation was rejected by the President on January 19, 1979. The Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules 1966 were amended by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by sub section (2) of Section 3 of the Act. The proviso to that sub clause provided that no person who has been previously appointed to a post in the service shall be eligible for appointment to the said post unless he has had a permanent job with the same qualifications and experience of the concerned subject. The respondent contended that the appellant had acquired the status of an Associate profess or of the Indian Medical Council and was entitled to the benefit of the proviso to sub cl. (2). The High Court held that the post was not a teaching one but it was a part of the cadre of the Institute. The High court held that since the post graduate research ers had been treated as a separate class, the appellant could not claim seniority or eligibility for promotion merely because he was working as an Assistant Professor. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. 1 The word " as " in the definition of " Director " in section 2 (2)( b) means " as defined in the Act ". [ 80 G H ] 1. 2 The word'as'in the context in which it appears, is used in the sense in which the word'may'is used. It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to a particular post. [ 80 F ] 1: 1 The expression " as specified in the First Schedule " must mean " in relation to " the person who is in the line of promotion. It does not mean " as described in the first schedule " and " in its place " and therefore, would not entitle the incumbent any special benefit with regard to any teaching. [ 81 B C ] 1; 2. 1 There is no order placed before us of the President of India directing that confer ral of honor ary teaching design ations on Special ists in the Will ing don 43 Hospital and the Safdar j ang Hospital would not entitled such Special ists to claim seniority / eligibility for promotions even though they are in the lines of Associate Professors and Assistant Professors. [ 82 E F ] 2. 2 In the instant case the appellant was not drawing a teaching allowance of Rs. 200 / p. m. and was not in the position of an Assistant profess or. The question whether the teaching experience gained by the appellant as Decision and Holding: (i) Whether the teaching design ates in the will be considered as a teaching faculty ? (ii) Whether a person who was already employed in a teaching hospital like the Ir win Hospital can be considered eligible for being considered for appointment as Associate Professor of Pharmac ology in Maul ana Azad Medical College. [ 83 A B ] 2: 2. The word is used as a term in the main part of section 2 of the, read with the second Schedule to the Act, must be construed to mean " In the capacity of " as mentioned in the Third Schedule to this Act. [ 84 D ] 3: 3.

The workmen of the Company, who were workmen of a company, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on various grounds. The High Court held that there was no justification for fixing the minimum wages at the rate of three months'basic wages and that the Tribunal committed an error in not placing reliance on the decision of the Supreme Court in Fr ench Motor Co. Ltd. vs Workmen,; and that, even if it was held that the claim for higher bonus could not be accepted as the same had been made by the workmen on the basis that they had been paid less than what was fixed by the Tribunal at Rs. 95 which was the average minimum wage fixed by this Court in the case of Fr ench motor Co. (supra). In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The claim for lesser bonus could be based only on the ground that certain clerical staff were being paid bonus which in effect, amounted to about six months'wages. [ 677 B ] 2. The question whether the bonus should be computed on the footing of dearness allowance or dearness allowance, was a matter of fact, not within the scope of the Act but was essentially a matter which could be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 678 F G ] 3. The Tribunal was right in holding that the bonus payable to the workmen was not a fixed wage but was a consolidated wage consisting of the two elements of basic wage and dearness allowance. The contention that the amount of bonus was not based on the actual working of the workmen and that there is no basis for making the difference between the permanent workers and the work done by the workman. [ 679 D E ] 4. The reference was answered against the workmen. The workmen appealed to the Supreme court. The Supreme Court held in the affirmative that the principle contained in the judgment of the High Courts was applicable to the present case. The award did not state that the workmen had agreed to exclude these classes of workmen in regard to payment of bonus. The appellant company was therefore entitled to its share of bonus on the principle laid down in the above case.

The appellant was a partnership firm. For the assessment year 1960 61, the Income tax Officer assessed him at Rs. 69, 886 / and on that basis he filed a return of income for the assessment years 1960 61 to 1960 62. In the return the Income Tax Officer stated that the Income - tax Officer had not given any reason for issuing notice under section 148. The assessee's contention was that the impugned notice was invalid because it did not comply with the requirements of section 151 (2) of the Act. Held, that the Commissioner could not have issued a notice under Section 148. He did not give reasons for coming to the conclusion that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. The Commissioner was satisfied that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice Under section 148, and that the assessee could not be said to have been guilty of fraud or misrepresentation.

The assessee was a partnership firm carrying on business in the State of Kerala. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for relief under Section 25 (1)( b) of which the assessee was not entitled to relief under the section. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had no right to claim relief under [ section 25 ] (4). Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was dis continuance of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned. The income of the year 1931 49 was assessed twice under the Act of 19 18 and again under the Income Tax Act of 1925. The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was the plaintiff in the suit. She filed a suit for partition and separate possession of her 1 / 4th share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu Family and that there was no prior partition between them. On appeal by the first appellate court, the High Court held that the property belonged to one's wife'and his two sons. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the plaintiff's share in'the coparcen ary property was the notice under section 22 and its non compliance bad to be made for the purpose of giving due and full effect to the fiction created by Explanation I to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1937. The appellant, a company in the State of Uttar Pradesh, was incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Under section 11 (2) of the, the Central Government had been authorised to make rules for the carrying on of the life insurance business of all insur ers and other activities connected with the life Insurance business. The appellant was appointed as a day time worker in the year 1948. In the year 1956, he was promoted as a clerk in the service of the Corporation. He retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on 31. 3. 1938. On his retirement, he became eligible to be in charge of the management of the Life Insurance business and was governed by the Life insurance business. By virtue of section 7 of the Employees'Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1960, the appellant was deemed to have been in charge and control of the said business. He was also entitled to retire on completion of 50 years of age. The respondent challenged the order of retirement before the High Court contending that regulation 19 (2)( b) of Chapter IV providing for the transfer of employees of the Insurance business to the Corporation was ultra vires the Central Govern ment. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Regulation 19 (1)( a) is violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [ 221 F ] 2. The Regulations framed under Chapter IV provide for the transfers of employees to the corporation and not to the employees of an establishment. They are all provisions relating to the process of transfer. Sub section (2), therefore, does not violate article 14 and it is unconstitutional. [ 222 G H; 223 A ] M / s. British Pain ts (India) Ltd. vs The Workmen,;, referred to.

The appellants addressed a letter to the President of India seeking to withdraw their writ petitions. The appellants wrote a letter on 20 February 1975, and requested that the matter be placed before the Chief Justice for hearing in a closed cover. The President of the Bar Association, who was also a member of the State Bar Association filed an affidavit stating that the Government had decided to take appropriate action in this regard. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letters were not binding on them and that they were not given any notice or opportunity to be heard in the matter. Held: (i) The letter did not bind the appellants. The letter was addressed to the Governor of Haryana and the Prime Minister's letter was sent to the Chief Jus tices of the States. The Secretary of the Union made no attempt to do so. The telegram did not confer any right on the appellants to have their case considered at the time when the order was passed. The question whether the letter was served upon the appellants did not arise because the appellants refused to accept the offer and the High Court proceeded on the basis that the letter did contain the letter and the letter. The Full Bench fell into error in accepting the apology. (ii) The letters written by the appellants were correct. The letters were correct and the appellants could not be allowed to see what was stated in the letter as the letter had been sent to them. The appellant did not make any allegation against the respondents nor did he show that the respondents had taken any action against the persons who would sup press the facts. The judgment is vitiated by non application of mind.

C. R. 353. (2) [ 1973 ] 2 SCR. P. K. Mittal vs Union of India,;, referred to. 2.
