The appellant was a Hindu undivided family consisting of his wife and two sons, who were the original f ounder and owner of what was known as'A us an Singh's estate. By a gift deed executed between the appellant and the Rul er, the appellant received a sum of Rs. 36, 396 / on account of the pension payable to him in respect of land revenue of the Jagir. The amount which had been paid regularly from year to year by the Government to Babu Har Narain Singh was revenue receipts. The Income tax Officer held that the income accrued due to the appellant as an income chargeable to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. He also held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The income tax Officer is a capital receipt and not taxable. [ 704 C D ] (2) The word " accrue " in the definition in section 2 (1)( a) of the Indian In com et ax Act means " a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue colle ctions after deducting costs of the Tahsil establishment. It does not mean a right which is acquired by a part of the income of a trust. [ 705 E F ] (3) The expression " derived " is not defined in the Act. The term " derived ", in the context, is not a term of art its use in the meaning of the term in the Constitution. It is not sy non y mous with form. [ 703 B C ] (4) The payment of pension is revenue receipt. [ 706 G H; 707 A ] (5) The nature of the payment is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 18 37 and, therefore, it is not agricultural income as defined in section 5 (1).

The appellants were appointed as Supervisors Grade'A'in various posts of Chargeman II. They were promoted to the post of Chargeman I on ad hoc basis and later on promoted as such. In the meanwhile, the respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated 2nd February, 1981 passed by the State Government under Article 309 of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the promotion of the appellants was not illegal and directed the Union of India through the Director General of Ordnance Factories to promote the appellants to the grade of Chargeman l on regular basis. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High Cour t. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. 1. The direct recruits who claimed promotion as Chargeman II must be treated as having been given a proper place in the gradation list of Supervisor'A '. [ 724 G ] 2. 1 The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 have in pur's u ance of the order of this Court dated 2nd Feb ru ar y 1981, but they are also entitled to get their present sal a ry re fixed after giving them notional seniority so that their present pay may be protected from the date of their actual promotion. [ 725 D E ] 2: 2. The promotions made by the respondents to the extent of the petitioners were irregular and had not been made on account of any reason whatsoever. [ 726 F ] 2 (i) The appellants of this appeal have in fact joined as Supervisors'A ', and were promoted as Chargeman I. The promotion of these persons was not based on the seniority list of Supervisors'B'and therefore, it is difficult to read in that order the same was not correct. [ 727 C ] 3 (ii) The promotion made by way of promotion to the higher post with effect fr om the date his junior was promoted cannot be said to be arbitrary or violative of article 14 of the constitution. [ 728 H; 729 A ] 3. 1 It is true that the appellants in the instant case have in no uncertain terms stated that they were given a fair chance of promotion. But the fact remains that they did not have any right to claim promotion retrospectively. [ 741 G H; 742 A ] 2.( iii) The promotees who claimed seniority over and above the petitioners in the writ petitions before the Madhya Pradesh High Court were granted promotion as soon as vacancies became available and th at the respondents were promoted. [ 742 G H ] 2 (( iv) The respondents could not be allowed to take advantage of the fact that the direct recruits were already in service as Supervisors. [ 743 G H, 744 A ] (v) The direct recruit ment of the respondents was not in accordance with the rules. [ 744 D ] 2,( a) The promotions were not to be made on the basis of a selection process. [ 745 G H ]. (b) The promotee's were not entitled to any p ay for fixation of seniority cum merit. [ 746 G H.] (c) The seniority position of the promotees was that they had not worked on the approved panel Decision and Holding: (a) There was no question of their being placed in the seniority lists of Supervisors. The promotees were not shown to have been promoted to offic iate as Chargeman Grade II on regular ising the post. [ 749 D E; 750 E ] (b). The direct recru ite es were granted promotions only when vacancies arose. [ 751 G H.

The Karnataka State Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators were operating in the State of Karnataka. A number of writ petitions filed by the employees of the Karnataka state Road Transport corporation challenging the grant of two permits to the Karnataka SRTC for plying buses from one to three. The High Court held that having regard to the rule of preference contained in proviso to section 63 (7) of the, the preference granted to the employees was not a right given to them under the proviso to Section 63 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the preference contemplated by clause (iv) of section 47 should be given preference over others who have been employed as a transport vehicle. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The scheme of the proviso is that the person who has to pay the permit fee must have been in the car hire business for a period of 2 years with the help of cars of indi genous make or vehicles obtained from elsewhere and should have sufficient cont acts with travel agents ho te li ers / airlines, etc., and should be economically sound or that they should be owning and operating five tourist cars and travel agents. [ 10 G H; 11 C ] (ii) The policy does not exclude the status of the operator of the bus which may be a transport service, but it is clear that the policy does n't cover the interest of the workers. It is difficult to accept the contention that any other interpretation would have w ip ed out the difference between sections 68 C, 68 D and 68 E. [ 11 F G ] (iii) The object of the Proviso to section 64 (7), is very clearly that the concession made by the State Government to the State Transport Undertaking should be limited to the number of permits to be granted. The proviso to sub section (1) of Section 63 makes it clear that if the State transport undertaking is required to comply with the conditions specified therein, the State Tourism Development Corporation shall be entitled to claim exemption from payment of the prescribed amount.

The respondent purchased a business in the name of the appellant firm. The business carried on by him was transferred to the respondent's sister concern. The respondent claimed that he had paid some amounts towards sales tax due from his predecessor in title, but there were arrears of sales tax payable on the sale of goods which took place before the transfer of the business under Rule 21 A of the Rules framed in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government by section 19 (1) and (2) of the Act. The Sales Tax authorities demanded the amount of sales Tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the goods. The appellants contended that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax because the respondent did not have any machinery for the period prior to the date of the transfer and therefore the respondent could not be liable to payment of sales - tax on the sales of goods effected by the seller of the said business. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the State government had authority under section 19 of the, and the rule making power under section 20 (1), and the rules made thereunder, under section 18 (c) of 1959 Act, and that the rule made under section 22 of the 1959 Act was ultra vires of the rule.

The appellant was appointed as a jail or an Assistant Jail or in the State of Gujarat. He was served with a charge sheet under section 7 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short'the Act ') and in respect of certain charges framed against him, he filed a written statement on September 4, 1954, denying the allegations made by him. The defence was that the appellant had committed a breach of article 311 (2) of the Constitution, as he was not supplied with a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer. The trial court held that the order of dismissal was illegal and void and directed the appellant to pay the arrears of salary and other benefits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach on the part of the respondent and that the failure on his part to furnish the report amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 of the constitution. Held, that the finding of the High court dismissing the suit was based on the quantum mer uit or contract and the court is entitled to give relief to the plaintiff if the defendant was found guilty of unfair labour practice. The High Court was right in holding in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not concerned with the second question whether the action was in accordance with article 311. The decision of the Privy Council in Re illy vs R. (5) applied.

The appellant, a land lord of the State of Bihar, filed a suit for possession of certain lands in his possession. The respondents claimed that they had encroached upon their coal mines and had rendered the remaining coal to the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal the High Court held that the respondent had encroached on the appellant's land as well as on the land which was not occupied by him. Held: (i) The burden of proof was on the respondent to prove that he had knowledge of the fact that the appellant had encroached into the land. The onus of proof would shift to the defendant. But the courts were not right in accepting the plea of limitation. The burden is on the plaintiff who asserts a right, and it may be, having regard to the circumstances of each case, that the defendant had knowledge or information about the same. [ 749 B C ] (ii) The onus is on a plaintiff who alleges a right and it might be having regard either to the facts of the case or the surrounding circumstances of the particular case. If he proves this, then the defendant has to prove the date when he knew that the property which he is seeking to recover was in his occupation. [ 748 E F ] (iii) The evidence adduced before the court showed that the construction of the mine was complete because of the appellant and the respondents. The appellant did not deny that the cement was still left in the encroached area. The High Court rightly rejected the contention of the appellants.

The appellant was a workman in the employ of the respondent. He was dismissed from service by the appellant and he filed an application under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders to dispense with his services. The Tribunal held that the appellant had committed misconduct and directed reinstatement of the appellant but it did not impose any punishment on him. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of discharge and directed the reinstatement of appellant. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The industrial tribunal has the right to inquire into the cause which led to the termination of service of an employee and has not been accepted by industrial tribunals over a long period of time even though it is not considered necessary for the purpose of determining whether the proceedings are or are not properly conducted. [ 828 B ] (2) The Industrial Court has the power to adjudicate upon the causes that led to termination of the service of the employee and have the effect of vitiating the enquiry. [ 829 C D ] (3) The employer could defend the action under r s. 18 of the standing orders if he had no opportunity to produce evidence before the court. The question whether the employer should take action under cl. 18 is irrelevant. The industrial court cannot go behind the finding of the fact that the employer wanted to take action for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. [ 830 E F ] (4) The domestic tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [ 835 G H; 835 A ] (5) The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came up before it for adjudication.

The appellant was the receiver of a building in the town of Ahmedabad. He had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the purpose of sub letting and for the purposes of the business. The receiver's were bound to enter into agreements with the parties, and that the respondent was bound to execute and register the deed of sale. The respondent filed suit No. 149 of 1960 against the appellant on the ground that he was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre and to exhibit cin emato graph films. The Trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court should have decided the question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or not. Held, that the expression " case " in section 92 of the Evidence Act means a civil proceeding and is not restricted by any law made by Parliament or to have been taken in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. It is true that the jurisdiction of the Court of m all court in England is confined to the matters mentioned in the section but it does not operate as res judicata between the parties. The word " case ", in section 96 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, means a suit instituted before the law of limitation, and does not include a part of the proceeding which has been expressly excluded by the Code of Civil Procedure. The words " case ". are wide enough to cover all cases where the facts are so clear that they cannot be decided by the Court. The expression " matter " is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. The Court can only decide whether a particular fact is relevant or not for determining whether it is a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code. The test is whether the document is a lease or of other character has to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent,'could not operate to determine what is the subject matter of the lis.

The respondent was appointed as a Clerk in the District Sol di ers Board in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. On 29. 3. 1985 he was declared fit by a medical board and was discharged from service on 30. 8. 1985. In the writ petition filed by him, the High Court held that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of termination. [ 245 F ] 2. The appellant was entitled to be in service till 30th of August, 1985 when the writ petitioner was reinstated in service. The true position is that arises on account of the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th August, 85, the respondent was entitled only to continue in service beyond 30th August. 1985 unless there was a further extension. Clause 6 & 7 of the first order of appointment stated that the respondent would be treated as a temporary Government employee during the period he was entitled under the terms of the officers mentioned in the said order. [ 246 G H;

The appellant was tried for an offence under section 302, Indian Penal Code. He was convicted and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him of the charge but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the conviction was not sustainable in law; (ii) the trial court had wrongly held that the prosecution version was more probable than the version of the prosecution; and (iii) the High Court erred in interfering with the order of acquittal. Held, that the High Courts were justified in interfering in the order passed by the trial courts. The view taken by the High Judge was correct. The reasons given by the Sessions Judge for acquitting the accused are: (1) the evidence of P. Ws. 4 and 5 is consistent with the innocence of the accused; (2) the witnesses have been won over by the defence; (3) the testimony of P W 1 has been totally unreliable; (4) the contradictions pointed out by the Trial Court were of a minor character and that they have been materially contradicted by the evidence on record; and, (5) the discrepancies noticed by the learned Sessions Judge were of such a serious nature which could not be explained by the accused.

The appellant was convicted under section 5 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 2, 000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the appe l l ant was not sustainable in law because he had been convicted by a Judge of the Supreme Court and his conviction was set aside. Held: (i) The expression " public servant " is wide enough to include Judges who are entitled to be removed from their office. The word " public servants " is not defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the word " person " means a person who has in his possession pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. It is for him to explain how the power to make an offence is given to him. A judge must be deemed to have been appointed by the President under article 124 (4). If he has in the possession pecuniary resource or property dis per sed, he cannot be said to have committed an offence within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section (1) of section 5 of the Act. (ii) The words " any person " in section 5 are not sy non y mous with " Judges " and " public officers ". The word'public servants'is not used in the sense of " public officer ", but it is used in a sense of a wider import than the ordinary dictionary of the word. [ 330 E F ] (iii) The word ` public servant'is used to den ote the act of a public servant which is entrusted with the task of interpretation of the Constitution and ensuring that the other two w ings do not over step the limit indicated in the Article. The principle is applied in the absence of statutory provision to the contrary. The doctrine is applied to the facts of the case as well as to the circumstances of the particular case. The test laid down in W ool ming ton vs Director of Public Prosecution,, approved.

The appellant was a member of the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khar gram constituency. He filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election of the appellant on various grounds, namely (1) that he belonged to the Ud ri caste which had no connection with Sun ri caste; and (2) that the appellant was not a member thereof. The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the respondent was a resident of the Ud ari constituency and that the question whether the appellant belonged to a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe was irrelevant. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The High Court erred in holding that as the appellant belongs to the Ak ri caste, the word'Lohar'in item 40 could not be interpreted as belonging to a tribal backward class because it did not belong to a tribe who formed the smaller caste group of Ja it. [ 389 E ] (ii) The expression " excluding Saha " in item 39 is wide enough to refer to any determin ate part of a caste consisting of a sur name, but not those within that caste who formed a separate caste distinct from the Sun ri castes. It is immaterial whether the word " except " is shown that it indicated a smaller caste groups of Sun ri tribes. [ 390 B C ] (iii) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that the Sa has included both the Ga us as an independent caste and the appellant having done so, the Tribunal rightly held that the dispute raised by him was not one of the constitu ents mentioned in item 41.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called " Ganga Vihar ", Marine Dri ve, Bombay. He was the first defendant in the suit and his wife was the second defendant in that suit. The appellant filed an application for leave to appeal under section 19 (2) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, LV II of 1947 for permission to occupy the building as care tak er of his flat, which was dismissed by the Presidency Magistrate. The High Court held that what was received by the appellant was by way of pu e li ment or surrender of the property and not a relinquishment. On appeal by special leave, HELD: The word'relinquishment'is not a term of art and is used in the section not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive meaning as giving up of possession of the premises. [ 422 E ] In the instant case, there was no such relinquishment. There was no abandonment in the sense that the tenant dis appeared from the scene completely knowing that he had no claim whatsoever over this flat and the appellant did not deny the fact that he was not ready to pay rent directly to the landlord.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was dissolved and in 1974 the undertaking became one of the divisions of Tata Sons Limited. In 1974 the company was dissolved. In 1975 the undertaking was dissolved by the company. In 1981 the undertaking vested in the company the management of which was dissolved on January 9, 1977. On the basis that the company had no " functional integral ity ", it was contended for the company that the new wage scales were fair and reasonable and that it would not be possible to adopt uniform rates of wages. It was further contended that the Company could not have been employed as an " industry " under the provisions of the Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Held, that the Tribunal erred in holding that the increase in the basic pay was to be made at the end of the year of its dissolution. The Tribunal did not go into the question whether the new scale was justified or not because the Tribunal found that the revised wage scales had always been changed from time to time. The change in the wage scales was not correct. The fact that the Board's employees had filed a petition before the Tribunal for revising the wage structure was not disputed. The High Court was right in holding in the appeal that the reduction of the wage scale was not justified.

The appellant, a sugar Works Ltd., was a company engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of goods. The respondents were employed by the appellant as its employees. They were retrenched from service on the ground that they had been working as such under the terms of employment. The workmen's claim for wages was barred by limitation. Held, that the appellant was entitled to relief under section 2 (vi) of the Act before it was amended in 1958. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under the Act. The High Court was right in holding that section 15 of the Industrial Disputes Act did not apply to the case.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pep su. He was charged under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence under section 465 and section 409 I. P. C. for having misappropriated the amount of Rs. 51, 000 which he had been illegally taken into custody by the appellant. The trial Magistrate held that the prosecution had failed to establish its case against the appellant and accordingly convicted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused was illegal as sanction had not been obtained under section 197 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that the evidence on record did not justify the acceptance of the prosecution case. Held: (i) The charge against the accused is not proved beyond doubt. The charge framed against him is not established. The facts found by the trial court were not sufficient to prove the charge. (ii) The prosecution was bad for want of sanction under section 196 (1). The sanction was necessary because the charge was in respect of his duty of obtaining signatures or thumb impressions of the employees before wages were paid to them. But if they did not show their signature or thumb impression, the sanction could be necessary. (iii) The sanction under Section 197 (2) of Cr. P., C. P.- I. L. R., referred to. (iv) The question whether sanction was required under section 198 (1), was irrelevant. The question was whether sanction under s. 197 (l) of Code of criminal Procedure was necessary.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore. It had its registered office in the former Cochin State and it had been carrying on business in Travancore State. The Income tax Officer assessed the income to be Rs. 90, 947 representing only the profit it made in the Madras State. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income tax, the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indi visible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax, it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside the Travancore State, but the High Court held that it was not liable to deduction under section 32 (1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The object of section 24 (1)( 1932) is to tax income " income " which is profits or gains of an Indian State or so di vide business in India. [ 260 F ] (ii) The use of these words does not circum scribe the proviso to Section 24 (2) (e) and the Explanation which defines " business " and requires the application of the proviso, which includes the explanation which excludes from profits and gains of any year under any other head in that year. [ 261 G H; 262 A B ] (iii) The word " income'is not used in the section nor can it mean business in British India. That is why the words " business in Federal India " are used in section 10. But the meaning of the expression " business ". is wide enough to include business in England. [ 262 C D ] (iv) The definition of total income as given in section 2 (15) (1), in section 24, refers to business in American law and in the case of Travancore State income, profits or gain of foreign exchange arising out of such business in any other country.

The appellant company was converted into a Public Limited Company to take over the business of the respondent company. In July 1947, the Company filed a petition for the issue of a certificate of fitness in respect of its age of retirement at 60. The Tribunal held that the age of superannuation should not be less than 60 and directed that the period between the date of retirement and the date on which the application would be made should be taken into account. The appellant challenged the order of the Tribunal by special leave. Held, that the Tribunal had failed to appreciate the fact that the appellant company had been converted into an Indian Company and that it had no right to retire after he attained the age. The question whether the age should be increased or not is a matter for decision before this Court in appeal. The test laid down by this Court is not very wide but is more appropriate. It is only where the Tribunal has found that in all cases the Tribunal could have given such a direction. The Court did not find any justification for the approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with the case.

The appellant company was registered in the year 1961 and had an authorised capital of Rs. 50, 00, 000. The Company filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Chairman of the Board dated May 19, 1965. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the order was made mala fide because it was made by the Chairman himself and not by the Board. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power of superintendence over the affairs of companies is retained by the Central Government in very wide terms and is capable of being exercised various ly. The power to call for information is conferred on the Reg is rar in two different ways. Secondly, the power to ask for information or explanation from the company and the President is vested in the Board and not the Board; and the Registrar has no authority to call upon the company to give notice to the company. [ 319 B C ] (2) The powers of the Registrar under section 234 are exercisable by the State Government in particular and subject to such control as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of the Act. The powers are entrusted to the Board under section 237 (b) of the. The Board can exercise its powers under section 235 only when there is a prima facie case against the company for violation of the provisions of the law. [ 320 E F ] (3) The Board's power to summon witnesses is not confined to the formation of opinion but is limited to the making of the order. It is not merely incidental to the exercise of the power but is capable to be exercised several ly. [ 321 G H ] (4) The order passed by the chairman of the company is not violative of article 14 and is liable to be set aside.

The appellants were convicted for the offence of dacoity and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of six months. The High Court acquitted them but reduced the sentence to three years'rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) There is no other evidence in the case which points to the complicity of the persons with whom the contraband was recovered. [ 721 C ] (2) The circumstances under which the one presumption or the other may be drawn are not stated by law and therefore it is necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the involvement of the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thi ef or the daco it. [ 722 E F ] (3) The fact that the accused did not have the gold biscuits seized at the time of the dacoity was found in their houses. The trial court and the Court below rightly held that the appellants were themselves the daco its.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a shop manufacturing only certain raw materials and not all sol ub les. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of Section 5 of the (Act) (which was repealed by the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The petitioners contended that the section is ultra vires the Act as it was not enacted in exercise of the power under the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the Act was not applicable to the other States. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 2 are not inconsistent with the scheme of the Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term would fall anything cal cu l ated to destroy life. [ 223 E F ] 2. The petitioner's right to carry on any trade or business cannot be said to come within the amended Rules. It is a law in force in the territory of India before the commencement of the Constitution and as such continued in force. The proviso to Rule 2 (x)( 2) of the Delhi Po sition Rules, 1926 is not violative of Article 14 of the constitution. [ 224 G H; 225 A B ] 3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poison for the entire country.

The assessee firm was a partnership firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. During the assessment year 1952 53, the assessee claimed allowance for Rs. 2, 68, 385 / due from the Bombay firm at the foot of its running account as a bad debt and claimed allowance in respect of the said amount. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer but allowed the claim on the ground that the debt had arisen in the course of business as che mis ts and d ru gg ists or sil k yam and it was not a case of the assessee's business as a banker or money lender or an off shore, but it was a case where the assessee had dealings with a firm known as " Bhoj aji Sob ha chand " (to be hereinafter referred to as the assessee) and the firm was carrying on business at Bombay as exporters. The High Court held that the sum of Rs. 1, 68. 385 / was not one incurred in the process of the appellant's profession as a bank or money lending business, and that the balance of Rs 2, 87, 8 O 7 / was the income of the firm which was disallowed by the Income tax Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee was entitled to the deduction of Rs 1, 87. 56 / was a question arising out of the question on which he was called upon to submit a statement of the matter. [ 423 C ] (ii) The Tribunal has come to the conclusion that the money received by the assessee to the Bombay concern was not an income earned in the ordinary course of the business of the assessees. It is true that the Tribunal has gone into the question of the fact on which they were required to submit the statement of a case. But the Tribunal did not give any findings on the points arising for decision. [ 424 E F ] (iii) The High court erred in holding that the cash credit taken by the appellant in the present case was not income earned by the respondent company. [ 425 G H; 430 A ] (iv) The finding of the tribunal that the moneys sent by the asses see were not loans made in the normal course of its business cannot be upheld.

The petitioners in these two writ petitions were the owners of certain lands acquired by the State Government under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. They filed applications for compensation and obtained an interim stay of dispossession. The High Court dismissed them on the ground that they had not been made within two years from the date of the publication of the declaration under Section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that as the awards were not made within a period of two years after the publication, the entire proceedings for acqu i sition of the land should lapse. Dismis sing the Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The special leave petitions are liable to be rejected. [ 823 E ] 2. The petitioners have moved the Supreme Court for interim relief in respect of their claim for compensation. The question whether the award could be said to be barred by limitation or not is purely a question of fact which has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 824 G H; 824 A ] 3. The Supreme Court in its judgment dated August 14, 1984, in the case of S. L. P. Nos. 823 and 824 of 1990, held that the question whether a notification under section 4 of Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was made within three years from September 20, 1984 cannot be decided in view of the provisions contained in section 11 A of the Bombay Act.

The appellant was employed in the Bank. He was working as a clerk in the Bombay Bank. In the year 1962, he was promoted to the post of clerk and his pay was fixed at Rs. 200 per month. On January 1, 1962, the appellant was appointed on November 17, 1964. He worked for about 8 years and after that he was given an increment of Rs. 150 per month on January 1. 1962. In April 1949, he made applications under section 33 C (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 praying for fixation of his pay by adding the scale of pay of Rs, 200 to the new scale of Rs., 180 to the old scale of the new scales of pay. The appellant contended that the scale should be revised from January 1 to January 31, 1960. Held: (i) The appellant's basic pay as on January 01, 1959 should be fixed at the rate of Rs 175 per month and should be entitled to two increments under sub cl. (ii) of cl. I of the Standing Orders. (iii) The High Court erred in holding that the appellant'was entitled to one increment under r. 14 (1)( b) of Part. IV of the Indian Industrial Tribunal (Bank ers'Association) Award ing the appellant to the scale prescribed by the Sas try award.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel, filed a suit for possession of their land. They claimed that they had been given up by the Government and that the agreement was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the agreements were void as they did not contain any provision for the grant of leases. Held: (i) The agreement was an act of oppression and the appellants could not be allowed to contend that the rights of the parties were extinguished or that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the agreements. (ii) The appellants'case was that the contracts were void because they were not in accordance with the terms of the lease. (iii) The agreements were not binding upon the appellants. (iv) The High Court erred in holding that the transactions were void since they were entered into without notice to the appellants and were not open to public auction. (v) The contracts were not enforceable under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (vi) The question whether the agreements are void able was not raised before the High Court. (vii) The contention that the right to sell property is not absolute but the right of the appellants to purchase the property is irrelevant. The appellants have acquired title to the property and the properties are not subject to ad judging the value of the property. The High Courts failed to notice the fact that the sale of the land was not a sale of a sale able right but a lease by the State. The agreement between the appellants was an action of oppression. The contract was not one for personal gain. It was only when courts were informed that the contract was subsisting that the land would be sold. The contracts must be held out. [ 240 G H ] (viii) The first appellant was a trade union ist and he was a trader. He was a member of the joint family. He had no interest in the business of the company. He did not have any interest in his own property. He never came into contact with the company nor was he a stranger to the company and therefore, the appellants cannot be heard to complain against the public auction and the High Courts should not entertain the petition.

The assessee was the kar ta of a firm carrying on business as grain till ers. The assessee had filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share in the property. The respondent claimed that he had been given Rs. 1, 50, 000 to his son and that he was entitled to the entire amount of Rs. 46, 560. The Income Tax Officer held that the sum of Rs., 1, 00, 000 was properly included in the income of the assessee. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that there was no valid gift. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that it was not proved that the transaction in question was bona fide but that the amount was available to the assessee who was authorised to hold the amounts on behalf of the done es which resulted in a valid gift and therefore the money received from the respondent was rightly included in his net wealth. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 10 did not apply to gifts of Rs.. 1 lakh and Rs. 50, 0001 made by the deceased to his sons and grand children. [ 128 G ] (ii) The decision of the High court is set aside. The High court was in error in answering the question in favour of the revenue. [ 129 D E ] (iii) The question whether the gift was valid gift or not was not relevant. The Madras High Court had taken into consideration the fact that the donor was a partner of a partnership firm having a half share in all the shares. The question was whether the said gift was legal and valid. [ 130 F ] (iv) The order and judgment of the Tribunal were set aside by the High Courts.

The Orissa Su perior Judicial Service (senior branch) Rules, 1963 were repealed by the Orissa Su preme Judicial Service Rules, 1962. Rule 2 of the said rules provided that " the High Court shall have power to transfer any officer from one post to another in the same manner as it has for the purpose of these rules. " By section 3 of the Orissa Special Judicial Service Act, the power to appoint a Registrar of the High Courts was given to the Government and the High court had no power to post him on the ground that he was subordinate to the Chief Justice. The High Court held that the power of appointment of the Registrar of High Courts under article 235 of the Constitution was not available to the government because the power was exclusively vested with the High Judge and the Supreme Court could not interfere with its functions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power to make appointments of officers of the special courts is subject to the control of the Supreme court. [ 156 E ] (2) The powers conferred on the High courts under article 236 are wide enough to include the power exercisable by the High Judges of the State and the executive authority of the state. They are not limited to judicial exercise of power. They cannot be exercised by the executive to post them to administrative posts in the ordinary course of things. It is open to the High. court to fix the period during which they may hold any executive post. [ 157 G H; 158 A B ] (3) The High court was right in holding that it had no jurisdiction to fill some of the posts in secret ari at by transfer judicial officers under its control. But the High C ount ing Officer who was appointed to the post of law secretary, did not act in such a way as to advance public interest. If he acted with that object in view as he was competent to do so, he could not have transferred the officer to his parent department. [ 159 F ] (4) The order of the high Court posting Shri K. K. Bose as well as Shri P. C. Dey as the deput y law secretary of the Su perior Administrative Tribunal, Chennai, were illegal.

It is clear that the parties have signed the compromise deed showing that a money of Rs, 1 lakh had been received later. [ 548 E F ] 4. The compromise petition shall be accepted and in terms thereof the suit shall be disposed of and the terms of the compromise shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this Court for disposing of the special leave petition. [ 549 G H;

The workmen in the two appeals were employed as a casual labour in the State of Gujarat. They claimed that they should be paid wages under the Act, but the claim was denied by the Tribunal on the ground that the Act provided for periodical payment to an insured worker in case of sickness (illness benefit) and not permanent disablement benefit. The Tribunal held that the provisions of section 99 of the Act did not cover all contingencies of sickness and that the benefits under the said Act could not be granted to the workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the benefit of sick leave was not available to the first two days'sickness benefit because the sickness benefit was given to the workers in the region. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The contention that the employees had been denied maternity leave is untenable. [ 10 E F ] 2. The question whether the benefit should be admissible to the workman in the matter of the grant of sick Leave has been examined in the light of the earlier decision of this Court in M / s. Hindustan Co oper vs Industrial Tribunal, Bombay,;, referred to. 3. The expression " sickness benefit " used in section 99 is not a bar to the demand of the workmen for sick leave being provided for the workmen in a particular industry. It does not in any way affect the question of sickness benefit. [ 11 E G ] 4. The words " sickness benefits " are not similar to those admissible under the statute. The Act does not provide for the grant or refusal of leave on full pay on the part of the employer. The word " sickness " is not sy non y mous with the present one. The term " sickness allowance " is a serious mis fort une to a workman for it cannot be equated with a workman who has been able to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. It is not merely a sudden sickness or suffering which may have occurred in the past. But it is not enough that the workman must have suffered from any other disease which he might have sustained while he was certified by a medical practitioner to be ill for that or a longer period. [ 12 E F; 13 B C ] 5. The definition of " sickness Benefit " in section 46 (1)( a) of the, does not include the leave of any kind due to sickness. The other question regarding the quantum of the benefit under the provisions Of the Act has been answered in the affirmative.

The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 18 61. He was arrested on the 9th June 1955 and was taken into custody by the police on the 10th June 1955. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to be furnished with copies of the documents which were relied upon by him as evidence against him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of detention was mala fide. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the grounds of detention were vague and did not contain any particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by the petitioner or the names of any of the persons aid ing the said petitioner. HELD: (1) The grounds must be clearly communicated to the detenu at least to that extent. [ 208 G ] (2) The mere fact that the detaining authority has stated in the affidavit that the petitioner is an accused person who is entitled to be supplied with copies, does not vitiate the order. [ 209 A B ] (3) The allegations made in the counter affidavit are open to challenge only when there is material to show that the statements made in paragraph 15 (g) relate to the particular period for which the petitioner was alleged to be making use of the statements. It is not necessary to mention these matters to enable the detaining authorities to make a proper representation to the Board. [ 210 E F ] (4) The expression " furnish particulars " in section 10 of the Act means a statement of facts which cannot be required to be disclosed. The expression'furnish particulars'is not defined in the Act. The word'furnish'is used in the sense in which the expression'furnishing particulars'in section 11 is used. The right to receive copies is subject to the limitation under article 22 (5). [ 210 C D ] (5) The right of the detenue to be given a reasonable opportunity of making a representation is subject only to the limitations set out in article 22. [ 211 H; 212 A ] (6) The power to disclose information is a part of the fundamental right to life guaranteed by Article 21.
