The appellant was a Panchayat and the Panchayat had filed an appeal against the order of the Panchayat. The Panchayat passed resolution No. 5 dated September 4, 1963, approving the octroi limits and the number of octroi duty to be levied and collected by the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the resolution on the ground that it was not a valid resolution under r. 21 of the Fees Rules, but only a declaration of the date of publication of the notice under r, 4 (b) of the Rules. Held, that the resolution was invalid as it did not contain any specific provision in the Act or rules relating to the levy of the prescribed rates. The resolution was passed without giving any opportunity to the appellant to raise the point at the time when the articles were sent for approval. The High Court was right in holding that the Panchayat could not dismiss the appeal of the appellant because the resolution dated March 25, 1963 was not in accordance with law.

The appellants were convicted under section 31 (1) of the, and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of six months. The appellants filed an application before the Conciliation Officer praying that they should be reinstated in service with effect from January 17, 1952, and that they had been dismissed by the Conciliation officer on December 31, 1951, and the High Court quashed the order of dismissal. Held, that the reference was not barred by section 20 (2)( b) of Act XIV of 1947. Section 12 (6) of The Act provides that where a settlement is arrived at after the report of the conciliation officer is received by the appropriate Government or where no settlement is reached, when the report is received, by the Appropriate Government, it would be open to the Government to consider whether the enquiry proceedings could be said to have commenced if the report was received by him.

The petitioner was detained under section 3 (2) of the, on the ground that he was in possession of illicit traffic and was likely to be released. He was also served with a notice of detention under section 9 (1) of that Act. The grounds of detention were supplied to him by the detaining authority but he did not give any hearing. The petitioner challenged the order of detention before the High Court contending that the order was illegal and without jurisdiction as the detenu was already in custody. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive detention cannot be justified because it is passed merely on subjective satisfaction of the detaining authorities. [ 910 E ] 2. The power of preventive Detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various enactments dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessit ating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his release, the power of detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of arrest was served upon the detenu, the detenu had surrendered for whatever reasons, therefore the order could not be justified. It is well settled in our constitutional framework that the power Of directing preventive detention given to an officer is discretionary in nature. [ 911 F G; 912 A B ] 3. The fact that the detenu may be released on bail does not vitiate the order. [ 912 D ] 4. The detention order itself is set aside. The writ petition and the special leave petition are allowed.

The appellant, a dealer in the State of Andhra Pradesh, was carrying on business as a money lender. He was found to be in the habit of taking business as such dealer. The High Court held that section 28 (6) of the Act did not provide for any guidelines or conditions or circumstances under which the Administrator could refuse permission or grant permission to a dealer. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the provisions of section 28 were ultra vires and invalid because they had been contravened by the proviso to section 28 of the Gold Control Act. HELD: (1) The object of the amending Act is " to provide in the economic and financial interests of the community for the control of the production, manufacture, supply, distribution use and possession of, and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " [ 10 64 D ] (2) The objects of the Amending Act are to provide for prevention of evasion of the other provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The main purpose of the amendment is to provide, in the social and economic interest of the people for the protection of the public interest, for the safety of the general public. [ 10 65 E F ] (3) The policy and scheme of the Acts are intended to prevent the legislature from being abused by the legis latures. The object is to enable the Parliament to make a comprehensive legislation to protect the public interests. [ 11 66 G H; 12 67 A ] (4) The legislative intent behind the enactment of section 27 (6), is to ensure that the Government has to give a hearing to the dealer who seeks permission to carry on his business as dealer but he is prevented only from carrying on the business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, orna ment or both. [ 12 69 C ] (5) The intention of the Legislature is to afford reasonable opportunity to the licensee to carry out the purposes of the legislation in making his orders. It is clear that the object of enacting section 28 is to facilitate the administration of the preparation, supply and distribution of, manufacture and supply of, essential commodities and business. [ 13 71 B ] (6). The object underlying the amending provision is to promote the development of the economy and to promote orderly growth and progress.

The appellants, who were the trustees of an alleged temple in the year 1954, filed a suit for possession of certain properties belonging to the temple. They claimed that they had been granted in Inam to the said temple by the respondent No. 4, and that the properties belonged to the Temple. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the property was his own and not his own. The High Court held that the appellants had established their claim of pres cri ptive title to the properties by adverse possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation as the appellants were not parties to the suit. Held: (i) The question as to whether the suit is barred by res judicata arose out of the decision of the High Court in G nan asam band a's case. The question whether the alien or must be deemed to have ceased to exist after the date when the alien ee was dispossessed by the appellant was a mixed question of fact and law, and the High court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below. (ii) The suit was within time. The appellants did not plead that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The suit having been dismissed on the merits, the appellants could not succeed. (iii) The appellants had proved their title to these properties by prescription. The burden of proof was on them to prove their title by adverse possess ory title. The plaintiffs had failed to establish their title.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was re constituted and a new partnership deed was executed by the partners of the firm. In the meantime, the appellant filed an application before the District Magistrate for permission to construct a cinema theatre at the proposed site. The said application was dismissed by the District Judge on November 11, 1982. The appellant thereupon moved the High Court under section 3 of the Jammu & Kashmir (Cin emato graph) Act, 1989 for permission in his favour as well as for grant of licence in his own name. The High Court held that the appellant had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema and that the order passed by the learned Single Judge was not binding on him. On appeal, the Division Bench set aside the judgment of the High court holding that the Letters Patent Appeal would stand allowed in conformity with the view taken by the subordinate courts. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated November 11. 1982 passed by a Single Judge dismissing the writ petition was violative of principles of natural justice. [ 586 G H ] 2. The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the Act as one inherent in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said section are present, the licensing authority had no jurisdiction to suspend the exhibition of cin emato graph films in the Theatre by persons other than the licensee. The impugned order was therefore, ultra vires. [ 587 B C ] 3. The mere reading of the District magistrate's order shows that it was not a case of suspension of the licence issued in respect of the Theatre. It was not an order which could be made by the State Government under section 4 of the, but was merely a direction to the licensing authorities to give a notice or hearing to the firm or its partners before he passed the impugned order. The fact that the District Collector had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order does not affect the validity of the law. [ 588 E F ] 4. The position would, of course, have been different if it was a case where the District Magistrates had no right to revoke the licence. But the question whether the licence had been granted to Ved Gupta or not would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If there was no such majority, then the decision of the Division bench would be inapplicable to the facts of the case. [ 589 D E ] 5. The appeal must fail.

The appellants were lessees of certain lands in the State of Bombay. They filed a suit for possession of their mills and factory to the effect that they had perpetual lease granted by the Custodian of E vac uee Property to them, and that the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 12 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that section 12 did not apply to leases granted by himself and that it was void as being inconsistent with the provisions of section 11 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 12 of which is applicable only to leases made without the express sanction of the Custodian, does not apply when there is no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that lease should also have been granted by him. [ 979 B ] (2) The respondent could not be said to have any authority under section 10 of the said Act.

The appellant, who was the father of the minor son of Raghubir Singh, filed a suit for partition and possession of his 1 / 3rd share in the property. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanum angarh by his order dated 10th August, 1972 declared that the father and the son constitute two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Big has and 16 Biswas only and the surplus land measuring 4 Big has & 6 Biswas may be resumed. The matter was taken up to the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan. The Board of revenue passed an order on 5th May 1976 declaring that the mother and the daughter were entitled to retain 127 Big has, and 16 / 7 Biswas should be determined according to the old law i. e. Act of 1955 and not according to old law. In pursuance of the direction of the Board, the Sub Divisional officer, Hanum ora, by his letter dated 5th May, 1976 held that the land in possession of the appellant herein was ancestral. The sub divisional officer, after hearing the parties, confirmed the order of the Sub divisional Officer. On appeal, the Board reversed the order and remanded the case to the Sub Division Officer, Naray ang ra. The appellant's revision petition before the Board was dismissed by the Board. The High Court set aside the order passed by the Sub division Officer and remanded it to the Additional Collector for fresh determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 221 of the Government of India Act, 1955 is not subject to the other provisions of the Act. It is clear from the language of section 221 of that the Board had power to make use of its powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board under the Act and the Board could not, therefore, make use or exercise of any power conferred by section 9 of the Land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not have made use of their powers of administration under section 9 Of the Land Reforms Act in regard to judicial proceedings. [ 728 G H; 729 A B ] K ana and others vs Board of Reven u er, Bihar,;, referred to. (2) The Board had by its order dated 14th April 1975 directed that the ceiling area for the appellant in law here in be determined by the sub divisional Officer on the basis of the old Law i. s. 11 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1973. [ 730 E F ] (3) The High court did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it go into it in detail.

The appellant was a public servant. He was not served with any individual notice by the Tribunal before he passed its award. The 1st respondent filed an application under section 33 (1) of the Act for setting aside the award, and the Tribunal dismissed it on the ground that the appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. The Tribunal held that the 1st respondent was not entitled to file an appeal against the award and that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the appeal as well as the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The expression'newspaper'as defined in the Act means newspapers which are used for publication of news papers or other media. It is not a matter of dispute that these decisions were given in the course of the decision of the High Court. [ 785 E ] The word ` newspaper'is not defined in section 2 (d) of that Act. The term ` newspaper ', as defined by section 2 of the said Act includes not only ` public news'but also ` comments on public news '. Every law report containing the judgment notes, and newspapers, including mag az ines, may be widely circulated in order to give effect to the judgment of the Supreme Court. The word'newspaper " as defined under section 2, is not sy non y mous with the word'news'and therefore, the expression ` newspaper " is not compreh ended within its meaning. [ 786 G H; 786 A B ] The expression ` news'is used in the definition of newspaper'in the context of the English Dictionary of the Indian Penal Code, which defines newspaper as meaning a newspaper. The Law reports which are newspapers and the employees employed by the public would be published by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. [ 787 C D ] The words ` news " and ` news print'have been used in conjunction with the dictionary meanings of the word ` news '. The Law Reports which are journals and the members of the public will be published in the official gazette. The employees employed in the newspaper establishments are persons who are citizens of India. They are citizens and citizens of the country. They constitute a substantial section of the society. They perform their functions in the manner they think fit to do. They do not act as newspaper.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises. He was a tenant and was a licensee. He had been described as the licensee and the licen sor. The appellant had been named as the " licen sor " in the agreement. It was alleged that the appellant continued to be the licensee for five years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st March, 1966. The respondent filed an ejectment proceeding against the appellant under section 41 of the Bombay Rent Act, 1949 on the ground that he was a lessee and not a tenant. The trial court dismissed the ejectment proceedings against the respondent. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licence was not put an end to by the appellant and that the respondent was entitled to continue in possession until the termination of his tenancy. Held: (i) The High Court erred in holding that the landlord was a lessor and not lease. The fact that the period of the licence had expired on 31st March 1966 did not affect the appellant's right to occupy the premises. The High court erred in interfering with the finding of the trial court that the defendant was a licence and not an " tenant " within the meaning of section 5 (4A) of the Act. (ii) The test of exclusive possession was important point. The intention of the parties was clear. The purpose of the agreement is to give notice to the licen sees and to the licensees to use the premises as a place of business. The licence fee was fixed. The licen sor was required to pay the rent for two months or if the licensee was liable to pay rent or mesne profits, the licen mer should have paid the rent. The license fee was to be paid by the licen cer at the time of the delivery of possession provided the licensee pays the rent regularly. The licensee shall not terminate the agreement after deducting all the dues if any for payment of rent or damages for breach of any term of the terms of the contract. [ 10 64 E F ] (iii) The object of the agreements is to provide for the establishment of a building or a building for the benefit of the employees. The agreement does not contemplate a lease. It is not necessary that there must exist a relationship between the parties. The terms of a contract are merely a matter of construction and the rights of the tenant cannot be determined by long process of reasoning. The words " licence " are used in section 52 of the E ase ments Act but the character of the transaction goes on the operative intent of the party. [ 11 64 H;

The appellant was a resident of the former State of Dholpur. He had been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling sugar in Rajasthan. On March 17, 1948, he applied for and was granted a licence for export of 15, 000 ma unds of ch uni's to be exported from the former States. The appellant applied for the grant of a permit for export ation of 15 000 ma ots for the year 1949. The application was rejected by the Central Government on April 23, 1950. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the State of Rajasthan was bound by the obligation of the latter State to pay the amount of excise duty for the quantity of 10, 427 ma unds for which the permit was granted. Held: (i) that the agreement between the Rul er of the Ajmer State and the Dalmia Dad ri Cement Company with respect to income tax and excise duty were not valid. (ii) that there was no recognition of the liability by the new sovereign and could not be enforced against the Rul ers. (iii) that even if there was any liability of the old States which did not represent the foreign State of the State, the State could not have imposed the liability of payment of excise duties because the rights of the subjects of the new States flowing from the old laws and were not subject always to the provisions of the Constitution. (iv) that since the United State of Bombay was formed by Co ven ant, the right to claim refund was taken away by the Rul ing of the Saurashtra State and therefore the question whether the agreement was a law or not would not arise.

The appellants were licensees of agricultural produce in the State of Madras and were granted licences at Koil ah. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act, and the Rules framed thereunder, contending that they were not liable to prosecution under section 7 (1) of the Madras Commercial Crop's Markets Act, 18 61, as they had not been registered as buyers and sellers, and that they did not fulfil the conditions of the licence granted to them. Held: (i) that the Act was void because the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the pro stitution of the price paid by it; (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the appellant was a trader in cotton and ground nut; and (iii) that he was entitled to be treated as a'dealer'within the meaning of section 14 of the Tamil Nadu Commercial Crop and Agricultural Department Act, 1952, and (iv) that section 14 (1)( g) of that Act was invalid because the levy of tax on the sale of goods was illegal.

The appellant was tried for the murder of one Ram chand, who was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 307. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The facts disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang's case. It is true that in the present case there is no evidence of any prior meeting. But it could arise and be formed again, as for example, by a systematic plan of camp ai gn, path ai gn and other things. [ 10 91 A ] (2) The fact that the deceased had died on the spot itself shows that he was guilty of the charge of common intent. [ 11 91 B ] (3) The circumstances show that the accused was guilty under section 326. The conviction was therefore only liable for the act of any of the others. [ 12 93 C ] (4) There was no evidence to show that there was any previous anim osity between the accused and the deceased. The prosecution cannot prove that his separate assault was a fatal one. [ 13 89 F ] (5) The circumstance that the appellant was guilty is not sufficient to convict him because he did not have direct knowledge of the incident. He must have been aware of the fact that he actually did. The incriminating facts must be in compati ble with the innocence of the accused. [ 14 G H;

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing. He was promoted to offic iate as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service with effect from 5. 11. 1976. On 3. 7. 1961 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating position and was con tin u ed by an order dated 8. 10. 1955. In the writ petition filed by him, he challenged the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that he had been prematurely retired by order dated 3. 8. 1961. The High Court held that the order was contrary to the express provisions of Rule 56 (j) of Fundamental Rules as also the power to compulsorily retire a public servant has been upheld by this Court. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner had not attained the age of 50 years by the date of the order. The order of voluntary retirement was passed. By 25. 5. 1954 the petitioner had already completed the age o 55 years by that time. Therefore, the petitioner could not be compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). [ 111 E ] 2. The fact that a person is in Class II or Class II service or post is not brought to an end by rever ting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of incap acity is exercised. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to classify Gov er nment servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) of Rule 57 (j). [ 112 F G ] 3. The object of Fundamental rule 56 (jj) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retiring a public officer in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into three categories covered under sub clauses.( i) to (iii) has a purpose behind it. If the con di tion indicated in sub clause. (i), is satisfied, namely, the Government Servant is in class I or Class III service or Post, whether permanently or temporarily or on officiating basis. [ 113 B C ] 4. The necessity for exercising powers under clause (j)( i) after he has attained the minimum of fifty five years of service by the order dated 5. 6. 1955, cannot be said to be a reasonable restriction on the right to pension and other benefits admissible under the rules.

The appellant Corporation was the husband of respondent No. 1 and father of respondent Nos. 2 to 5, who were the wife and father respectively of respondent NO. 1. Respondent No. 2 was the owner of a policy which was issued by the Life Insurance Corporation of India for the period from April 1, 1960 to 23rd December, 1961. The deceased had obtained two cheques for Rs. 300 and Rs. 220 respectively in favour of the appellant Corporation. The appellant corporation had also claimed the said amount and the appellant corporation by its separate written statement described the liability of the respondent Corporation on 28th January 1961. On 16th January 1961, the widow of the deceased filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of the amount due in respect of the amounts paid to her. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the claim made by the respondent corporation was not true or false; (ii) the proposal was not accepted and as such there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation; and (iii) the appellant had failed to prove that the proposal sent by the deceased was for some reason or other not accepted by the Divisional Manager of the Corporation. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i)( a) The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the late and the LIC. [ 353 B ] (b) The question whether the final contract was binding upon the deceased or the LIC must be answered in his favour. [ 354 C D ] (c) The decision of the Subordinate Judge is clearly erroneous in law because the question whether a concluded agreement would be concluded only when the party to whom an offer is made says or does something to sign ify his acceptance. [ 355 G H ] (d) The expression " under writing and revival's " in the Financial Powers Act, 1960 dealing with the financial powers has been used in Marine Insurance. It is clear that the expression " Under writing and Re vi val's of policies in case of Life Insurance Corpn. Of India Standing order, 1960 (Financial Powers) applies, if any, to an acceptance of the proposal. [ 356 E F ] (e) The word " under write " sign if ies accept liability under. The dictionary meaning also indicates that.

The appellant, a public limited company, was prosecuted for the offence of cheating and defraud ing the Government of India. The trial court held that the appellant had committed an offence under section 13 (1)( c) of the Letters Patent Act, 1947, and directed the filing of a complaint against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the High Court amounts to a judgment or decree which did not finally dispose of the suit or proceeding but was an interlocutory order within the meaning of article 133 (1) (c) and therefore, the order passed by the High court in the present case amounted to a decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in the suit. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (Per Shah, J.): (i) The order refusing interim injunction was not a final order within section 109 (a) of Code of Civil Procedure. [ 10 E ] (ii) The power of the court to grant interim injunction is exercisable only when the court has made an order deciding the question of law or the nature of the subject matter of the dispute in dispute. It is not necessary that the court should have regard to the matters in controversy in the suits or proceedings. If after the order is made, the suit is still pending, then the court will be deemed to be final. [ 705 C D ] (iii) The High Court erred in holding that the application for interim relief was incompetent because the plaintiff's suit was dismissed by the trial court. [ 709 F ] (iv) The appellant was entitled to interim injunction as he had committed the offence charged. The order dismissing the appellant's application was not an interlocutory one. [ 710 G H; 711 A ] (v) The orders were not appealable under section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Courts were right in holding the order directing the filing thereof. [ 712 B ] (vi) The jurisdiction of the Court to grant the certificate was not barred by article 133 of the Constitution.

The respondents, the manufacturers of cotton yarn and other intermedi ates, were also liable to pay excise duty on the fabrics manufactured in their factory. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of such goods sold by them and that the price at which they had been sold was not the price for the processed fabrics but was merely a price at the factory gate. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 provides that where the manufacturer is selling the goods in the course of manufacture or job work, he shall be entitled to include the process or as to what would be his price at whose value the processed tex's are manufactured. [ 345 F ] (2) The price at wh ate lling should be the price or deemed price at that place. [ 346 D ] (3) The wholesale price at this factory gate cannot be the sole consideration for the processing of the grey cloth.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the Panchayat Samiti, who was respondent No. 1 in this appeal. He was promoted as a Head Clerk on April 1, 1975 and was confirmed in that post on April 25, 1973. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted to the post of a Head clerk. In January 1974 he was appointed by the Panchayat. The appellant challenged the validity of section 33 of the Punjab Panchayati Raj Act, 1973, which provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1. 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the Amending Act shall continue to be governed by them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) It is clear from the language of section 13 of the amending Act that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the said post of the head Clerk. [ 737 G ] (2) The appellant had been appointed as an officiating clerk in a Panchayat and not being a part of the State Government service or retired in any other capacity. [ 738 D ] (3) The fact that the petitioner was promoted on April 21, 1975 cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into force. There is no substance in the contention that the right to be consider for promotion was a term and condition of service, because it was relevant for the purpose of the rules framed under the Act.

The appellants, who were the kar ta of the Math Sa una or the deity, filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math and was his personal property. The plaintiffs claimed that the properties in dispute belong to the math Sa una and that Mahant Shiv sh ankar Y ati was the che la of Mahant Shiv h ankar G okar an Y ati. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the Ama uli properties had been purchased by the father of the plaintiff as a personal property of the Mahant and that the said Raja was not a regularly constituted Mahant of the math. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the income from the properties belonging to the temple was not his personal and separate property and that he was entitled to be treated as a'personal property'in the hands of the deity and that his claim was not liable to be regarded as property belonging to him. HELD: (i) The fund from which the Ama ul properties were acquired constituted the personal property Of the Mahant, the burden of proof cast on the defendant who makes the claim. [ 663 B ] (ii) The High court has found that the claim was made by the Kar ta of a regularly appointed Mahant of Math Sa ila and Sar bar akar of the idol. The evidence shows that Mahant's share in the properties belonged to him and does not form part of the properties of the Temple.

The appellants were granted quasi permanent allotment of land to the respondents in the village Rai kot. They filed an application for review of their order cancelling their allotment on the ground that they had been wrongly allotted to them by the Custodian General, Punjab. The Additional Custodian allowed the application and cancelled the allotment of the land. The appellants then moved the Deputy Custodian General for calling up their review application and for revising the order of the Additional Custodian. The Deputy Custodian accepted the revision application and restored the allotment. The respondents appealed to the Custodian. On the question whether the cancellation was a result of mis apprehension of actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of sub urban land at all, HELD: (1) The power conferred by section 19 (1), is a general provision and the particular provision regarding cancellation of allotment is section 19. [ 337 B ] Bal Mukund vs The State of Punjab,;, followed. (2) The rule does not apply to a proceeding before an authority created by the, and not to an authority constituted under the Act. It is well settled that the rule applies to a proceedings before an Authority created by or under the, Act. The rule is in Chapter X headed " Payment of compensation under section 10 of the Act ". Therefore, it cannot be said that section 19 of the 1954 Act is totally in conflict with section 10. [ 338 F G ] Bal Shankar vs The state of Punjab;, applied.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Teachers in the State Government Schools and they were selected by the Public Service Commission. They were appointed on the basis of a written examination held by the State Public Service Commis sion, which was in two stages written and interview. The recruitment process was started in the year 1981 and the recruitment process commenced in 1982. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the decision of the Public Services Commission to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of the recruitment examination. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written test and the main question was whether the selection made by the Selection Board was vitiated by any irregularity or illegality. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in the month of May, 1985. The employment notification was in three stages written & interview / personality test. After the written examin a tion was over, the candidates had to be interviewed. The result of the written exam's was not declared. The selection of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates had become final and would not be disturbed. [ 125 E F ] 2. The State Public Services Com mission cancelled the entire selection process. On the other hand, the situation could have been fully properly met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the same footing. [ 126 G H; 127 A B ] 3. The situation could not have been conveniently ignored. [ 128 C D ] 4. The practice could have continued even after the written tests were over. The candidates who had better performance in the Written Examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce were not only called for interview but were also finally selected.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the respondent, filed a suit for possession and management of the D era in respect of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had no knowledge about the death of Som Dass as he was not impleaded as a party to the suit and that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The suit was filed on the basis that the appellants were not entitled to manage the properties of the C. P. The suit against Som Dass was dismissed. [ 489 B ] (2) The question whether the interest in the subject matter of the suit devol ved upon him is a question which could be raised only when the court decides the question whether there was any need for his impleadment or whether the dev olution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. Order 22, rule 10, is not confined to dev olution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mut t or manager of the temple res igns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head would be substituted as a parties under this rule. [ 490 F G;

The petitioners were appointed as Junior Engineers in the Secretariat premises of Andhra Pradesh. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer on January 9, 1983. On February 8, 1983 they were granted promotion to the next higher Grade Service from 58 years. In the meanwhile, the Government issued a notification dated October 29, 1979 and brought into force the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. By that notification, the age of superannuation was increased from 55 to 58 years and by another notification dated November 10, 1979, the State Government had decided to reduce the age to 55 years. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification before this Court by way of Writ Petitions Nos. 42 and 54 of 1969. The main contention of the petitioners is that the proviso under article 309 read along with Article 314 (1) of the constitution was ultra vires the Constitution and therefore invalid. It was also contended that the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules was not retrospective in nature but was prospective in operation. Allow ing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1). The proviso to rule 2 which conferred a right upon the employees to continue in service after they have passed the point of pe ak performance cannot be questioned as unreasonable or arbitrary and consequently violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constit ut ion. [ 582 E ] (2) The power conferred by the proviso is subject to the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The power to amend these rules vests in the Government. The proviso does not confer any power on the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and it is open to the Legislature to prescribe conditions which are necessary for the exercise of its powers under the proviso. [ 583 G H; 584 A B ] (3) The proviso is added to rule 4 which confers a power on Parliament to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and if no reasons are so stated, as appear from the language used therein, the power can be exercised by the President in accordance with the provisions contained in the proviso and when the Governor has exercised his power under the Proviso to Article 310 and if there is no reason why he should not follow the procedure prescribed by the Proviso.

The appellant, a registered dealer in the State of Haryana, purchased certain raw materials in the state with the aid of'manufactured goods '. He sold the finished products to dealers who in turn exported those goods out of India. On these facts, it was claimed that the sales were not exempt under section 6 (1) of the Act and that they were liable to pay tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9 (1). The Sales Tax Officer disallowed the claim for the purchase tax on raw materials which had been levied under section 8 (1)( b) of that Act. The assessee filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the High Court held that the purchases made by the appellant were not exig ible to tax under section 5 (1), but the question whether the sales of the appellant amounted to manufacture within the meaning of section 2 (e) of C. S. T. Act, 1956, was decided against them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The definition of'turnover'clearly indicates that goods are either to be taxed at the point of purchase or sale and the same transaction cannot be taxed as a sale in the hands of the dealer who sells to the assessees and as a purchase in the own hands of assessees. The only exception is the limited class of goods covered by section 9 but even this exception has been left out with complete retr o pr n ent of section 14, because, the taxable event does not fall under section 3 (1); (ii) The expression'export'in section 2 sub section (c) of section 5 of the C. P. T., Act, 1957, means " any person who deals exclusively in goods specified in Schedule B ". [ 348 G H; 349 A ] (iii) The Explanation added to section 2 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1948, makes no difference between the two provisions of the section and the proviso es inserted in section 24 (1).] [ 349 F ] (iv) The explanation added to the clause by the Finance Act, 1990, does not apply retrospectively. The Explanation applies retrospectively.

The appellants were the dealers of goods manufactured by them. They claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton and cas tor oil of the total value of Rs. 6, 47, 509 1 6, as mentioned above. The Sales Tax Officer rejected their claim for exemption on the ground that they had been despatched to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by them and that the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of the notification. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of assessment but held that the purchasers were liable to pay purchase tax under section 10 (b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the words " a registered dealer " in section 8 (b), " a person " in Section 8 (c) must be construed to have the same meaning as in section 2 (d) of that Act. Held: (i) that the expression'registered dealer'in section 9 (b)( ii) is wide enough to include a registered trader and an unregistered dealer. It is well settled that if the seller takes the bill of l ading to his own order and parts with it to a third person the property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. (ii) that in the absence of special agreement the owner of the goods has the intention to comply with the condition and to agree as between himself and the purchaser who is not a registered dealers.

The respondent wife filed a suit for maintenance against the appellant and his brother, who were the widow of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had no right to receive maintenance allowance from her husband and that she was not a divorce e. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the courts below had wrong in law in holding that the respondent was a divorce under section 125 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 which also included the payment of maintenance amount of Rs. 300 / for the son and Rs. 400 / for a daughter for their maintenance. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " divorced wife " is defined in section 2 (3) of The Indian Div or ce Act, 18 78. [ 79 E ] 2. The definition of " divorced woman " in section 125 of the Indian Penal Code is wide enough to include the word'child'in the definition of'divorced woman '. The term'divorced wife'has definite meaning and con cise ly used the term'married'as defined in the Act. [ 80 F G ] 3. Section 125 (3)( b) does not apply to the present case because the respondent herself had forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree obtained by her in the course of the proceedings. [ 78 C D ] 4. The husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case is that he had refused to pay maintenance allowance and the marriage was not proved. [ 77 H; 79 A ] 5. The fact that the mother of the respondent had given allowances to her, does not make the appellant liable for maintenance. Payment of me har money, as a customary discharge, is within the cogn isance of that provision. But what was the amount of me hal, it is not necessary that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s. 125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law applicable to the parties.

The appellant was the highest bidder in respect of a shop at village Re pura, P. S. P usa, District Samastipur. He was declared to be the highest bid for Rs. 11, 900. The Collector of the district after scrutiny of the application and after hearing the appellant, passed an order on 25. 3. 88 cancelling the bid of the appellant. The appellant challenged the said order by way of writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no requirement of giving any notice as required under Rule 9 (1) of the Bihar State Government's Rules, 1971. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) The order dated 25th March 1988 of the Collector is not set aside. [ 869 E ] (ii) The appellant had been given due notice and an opportunity of making representation against the order. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there were no requirement specifically of giving notice and that the appellant was also at liberty to pass any order in accordance with law. [ 870 G H; 869 A ] (iii) The fact that the rules do not express so, does not affect the future business of the person concerned in any event.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent firm, was inducted into a building known as'A'in the City Ten ants'Protection Act. He was converted into a partnership concern of the appellant firm and its partners. The rent was paid by the appellant to the respondent company on 30. 7. 1953. The appellant filed an application for fixation of fair rent under section 10 (2)( vii) of the Rent Controller Act, which was dismissed by the Rent Control Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to determine the question whether there was denial of the right to the property or not. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the nature or character of the suit lands must be held to have been ex facie wrong. [ 549 E ] (ii) The expression " estate " is defined in section 5 (1) of that Act to mean any land held by a landlord. It includes all land held at a time when the landlord is a tenant. The word " estate ", in the context of the definition of " estate ". has been used in the Act to include a Court of Small Causes disposing of an appeal from him. The words " estate of the deceased " are not defined in the Rent Act. They do not refer to any of the categories mentioned in section 10. [ 550 G H; 551 A B ] (iii) The term " estate'is defined to mean a tenure in respect of certain pre cin cts. It means a tenure of the landlord. [ 551 C D ] (iv) The terms of the lease deed clearly show that the lessor was entitled to recover the rent from the tenants. The respondent did not challenge the validity of the order in further appeal or revision before the High Court.

The petitioner was given due opportunity to make a representation against the final list of officers on an integrated seniority list. He filed a petition in the High Court challenging the tentative list and also the writ petition. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal, it was contended that the petitioner had no right to challenge the final gradation list as he had not appeared before the Court when the final lists were prepared. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner's petition was disposed of by the High court on the basis of an apparent mis de mean or. The fact that the Mysore State Civil Services Inte gr ation Rules 1960 provide for filing objections only against the preliminary list is not in dispute. [ 829 B ] 2. The petitioners have a right to represent before the final select list. They are entitled to an opportunity to object to the proposed issue ment of a place to them in the seniority list, and if they are aggrieved by non compliance with the procedure prescribed by law, they must be heard after giving them further opportunity to the concerned officers to make their representations. [ 830 E F ] 3. The principle enunciated in Sank ari ah's case (supra) is applicable to the present case. [ 831 G H; 832 A ] 4. The principles laid down in the decision of this Court in Shri Bhagwan and Anr. vs Ram Chand & Ors.,; applied.

The petitioners, who were licence holders in respect of certain goods imported by them under the Import Policy 1978 79, filed writ petitions before the Bombay High Court challenging the validity of the said licences. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions and held that the licences issued to the petitioners were valid for import of items which were exempt from import duty. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the petitioners had failed to establish that they and the Export House were similarly situate and that the expression " whether canal ised or otherwise " contained in the order dated April 18, 1985 did not include " whether the canal ised items could be imported directly by an Export House. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The licences issued in favour of M / s. Suraj Di amonds Industries Ltd., are granted by the Import & Export Policy 1988 91 and the export companies have been granted a licence under the Imports & Exports Policy 1988 92. [ 236 G ] 2. The petitioners have failed to make out a case for interference by this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. [ 237 E F ] 3. The orders of confiscation and redemption imposed by the Collector of Customs are set aside. The Collector of Central Excise and Customs, is directed to grant the appellants'licence afresh after granting the same. [ 238 D ] 4. The appeals are allowed.

The appellant company was a division of Mc Dow ell & Co. Ltd., which was, in turn, merged with the assessee. In the year 1981, the appellant company had filed its price lists in respect of the same product and the appellant had filed their price lists for the same. In this list, the assessee claimed that the cost of packing could not be included in the assessable value. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant did not collect any amount in excess of the amount indicated in the price lists. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had failed to prove that the price of the dr ums supplied by the buyer was entered in the RG 1 Register maintained for the goods manufactured by the appellant. On appeal, the High Court held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the seller, and therefore, the cost incurred by the manufacturer could not form the assessable values. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the value could not have been included in determining the assessable Value. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The expression " cost " in relation to packing in the clause (i)( a) means cost of such packing as the price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessable price. [ 980 B ] (ii) The word " cost ", has a definite connotation, and is used generally in oral or in ver n ac ular language, and does not mean something more than what is required by the statute. It cannot be said that the words " cost of packaging " in section 4 (4)( d)( i) of the Act are wider than the words'cost'in section 4A (4) (d)( ii). [ 981 D E ] (iii) The use of the word " Cost " in Section 4 (2)( d) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 is not restricted to the manufacturing activity of the assessee but is only incidental to the supply of the goods. [ 981 F G ] (iv) The words " costs of packing " in the sub section are wide enough to include the cost towards the cost.

The appellant was charged with having committed offences under section 161, I. P. C. and section 336 5 (2) read with section 5 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He was tried by the Special Judge for trial and convicted and sentenced to undergo R. I. for 15 months under section 5 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there had been no independent evidence regarding the demand, the mess enger who had accompanied PW 1 to give the notes to the appellant, did not have any direct evidence regarding demand, and that the appellant had not been examined in his personal custody. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i) There had been a clear indication that Ex. P 2 memo had been issued on the basis of a complaint received from the appellant that on getting the explanation from PW 1 he had given the money for the Dip awali. The case of the appellant is that he had made the demand and had also received the amount on 22. 10. 1975 itself. It is therefore not correct to say that there has been consistent explanation for the appellant. [ 338 F G ] (ii) The appellant had admittedly received the money as soon as he was arrested and returned to India. The appellant could not be said to have taken such a plea at the time when he was released. The fact that he was present before the seizure was not that of a loan transaction but payment of an advance of Rs. 125 in the canteen when the appellant started to take food there. The position was clearly in the course of the trial was not the same as the one in which the appellant was acquitted.

The petitioner company was a public sector undertaking. It had its registered office at Bombay and the Company purchased a sp acious flat being flat No. 151 in Jo lly Mak er Apartment III, P. W. 630, of which the company purchased a sc ent able flat bearing No. 150 in Jo ber Mak er Apartments, a plot No. 153 in Jo thee Mo g ul Line Limited, Bombay. The company purchased another sp acious apartment in Jo ther Mak er Tower III, which was owned by the company. In 1975 the company sold a sp ous al flat being Flat No. 115 in Jo ose Mak er Villa III at 119, C uff e Parade in Bombay for use of its senior executive, we should construe that it is not only the present officers and employees of the company but also to be treated as employees of a company who allowed to continue to live in the company's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement. The petitioner has been given one month's notice under section 80 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to show cause why he should not be removed from the premises of a director or employee of a Company within the meaning of section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of sub section (1), (2) and (3) of section 629 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the special leave petition and held that the view taken by the High Court was correct. Dismis sing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: (Per K. B. Gaj end rag ad kar, J.): (i) The expression " any such property " used in cl. (b) of sub sec.( 1) includes a right to possession of any property of a person other than a company. [ 637 E ] (ii) The word'past'means'an act of God '. The word ` past'refers to a particular act or thing. The word " past " refers to the existing officer or employee. But the word'or'does not mean'an individual or a group of persons ', but includes a person or a body of individuals, etc. The term'past ', refers to'an activity'which is an offence under section 630 (l)( b). The word is not defined in the Code, nor is there anything in the context in which it appears. [ 638 G H; 639 A ] (iii) The words'any such thing'in cl s. (a) and clause (b), are separated by the word ` or'which must in the sense in which they refer to the new officer or employees of that company. Therefore, the word " or " occurring in cl.( b) cannot be read as'and'and so construed, must mean withholding of property illegally obtained by an existing officer / employee.

The appellant, a Hindu religious trust, was the trustee of a temple. He was a public trust under section 2 (13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The appellant and his family members were trustees of the temple. The temple was represented by an advocate who had been appointed as a manager of the said temple. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the temple was not a public endowment. Held, that the appellant was a private trust within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. The deity was a charitable trust within section 2, (13), and therefore, could not be regarded as a public Trust. The definition of'public trust'in section 2 is wide enough to include all endow ments which are made from time to generation to generation on the strength of this writing out of love the below mentioned property valued at Rs. 600 (Six hundred) without taking any consideration from you for the purpose of expenses of performing worship and offering Na iv ad ya festival. The word'public'has not been defined in the Act and therefore the expression'public temple'must mean a public temple or a wakf.

The appellant, a mill of the Bombay Port Trust, was employed in the State of Bombay. He was employed as a man on daily wages in the Mill and Vict oria Doc ks at Bombay. On the day when the two shift system started, each shift system was extended to the Prince's and Vict ory Doc ks. The appellant was employed by the mills for more than four hours on any day. In April, 1949, the workmen were working in the factory. The workmen were paid a fixed allowance of Rs. 1, 000 per month. The Labour Court held that the Union had under its control several doc ks and it was not able to establish that the existing system of work was not extended to them. The Tribunal also held that there was no evidence to show that the new system of working was extended or that the work was done by the workmen. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the fixing of the two hours was not justified because the number of hours was increased from time to time. The words " ordinary rate of wages " in section 16 (2) (c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest and this is clear from Rule 24 (2). There is no definition of interval either in the Act or the Rules but the provisions of section 13 are not applicable.

The appellant tenant was let out to the respondent landlord for a period of 10 years. The suit was filed for eviction after the trial court decreed him on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and was entitled to protection under section 20 (1) of the Act. The Rent Control Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal, but the High Court set aside the finding of the trial judge and restored the decree. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that since the suit was not maintainable because the suit had been filed within the limitation, the bar of section 20 could not be attracted as the suit has been filed beyond the period of limitation. Dismis sing the appeal and condoning the delay, ^ HELD: 1. The right of the landlord to evict a tenant has been provided in the Act itself. [ 165 G ] 2. The provisions contained in sub section (2) of Section 2 of the Delhi Urban Buildings (Regulation of Let ting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 are applicable to the present case. The restriction on the right of a landlord to eject a tenant is provided for in this Act under Section 20 of the New Act. [ 166 B C ] 3. The provision contained in Section 40 will come into force only after the expiry of the period specified in the section. [ 167 D E ] 4. The language of Section 39 does not make any difference whether the Act applies or not.

The appellant was a th ika tenant. He was the landlord of the premises in suit. In the notice to quit served on him he had not been given any notice of termination of his tenancy right, and therefore he could not be said to have acquired title by adverse possession. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant who was the first defendant. The trial court decreed the plea of the appellant that he had failed to establish his rights as a th ila tenant. The High Court held that the appellant had not erected the structures on the land and was not a successor in interest of the tenant but only a transferee. Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent had not established any of the grounds specified in section 3 of the Act. The appellant having failed to prove the existence of one of the ground specified in Section 3, the respondent could not claim the benefit of section 4. The decision of the High court is therefore set aside.

The appellant was appointed as a Stenographer in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as per the recommendations of the Pay Commission. He was promoted to the post of Section Officer on January 1, 1973. He filed an application before the State Government for grant of pay scale equal to that of Section Officers and prayed that he should be placed at par with Section Officers. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the classification made by the State is not discriminatory and it has been done arbitrarily. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. It has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for. [ 250 F ] (ii) The differentia based on the experience is one which is more reliable than the work of the post and responsibility cannot be fastened with the duty to see that the under privi leg ed or weaker sections get their dues. [ 251 G H; 252 A ] (iii) The principle of " equal pay for equal work " applies to all persons who are left out. Those qualities or char ct er rating must, of course, have a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved. [ 252 B C ] (iv) The distinction between the two classes of posts and the nature of work done by the Bench Secretaries Grade I is also a reasonable differentia.

The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the, the Madhya Pradesh Land and Development Act, 1961. The appellant Company was a State Government undertaking under section 65 of the Madhya Bharat Area Development Authority Act, 1973. The State Government issued a notification dated January 28, 1976, which provided that the Development Authority shall make provision for the compulsory acquisition of land required for the purpose of the development plans and z oning plans with a view to ensuring that town planning schemes are made in a proper manner and their execution is made effective. The respondent 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the demand on the ground that it had no authority to levy tax on lands or buildings or both. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The expression " any other law " used in section 133 of the Transfer of Property Act means a law relating to land and building or part thereof. [ 10 G H; 11 A ] (ii) The definition of " land " in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, does not include property tax. The word " land'has been defined in section 3 (d) of the Act as meaning land and includes all land, including land or buildings. The term " land ", in section 4 (2), refers to property tax, and therefore, the power conferred by the said section will become in effect ual. The expression'land'in section 12 (2) is not confined to property taxes but is wider than those mentioned in the section. [ 11 B C ] (iii) The word'land ', in section 13 (2)( b) of Act, includes all lands. The words " land revenue " have reference to property Tax. The Commissioner of Sales Tax, Kor ba, who was authorised under section 5 of the U. P. Act, 1948, to exercise the powers and perform the functions under the Act, did not refer to the land revenue payable to the Government. The fact that the Act did not contain any independent provision or machinery for exercising the power of taxation, cannot be held to be irrelevant. [ 12 F G ] (iv) The decision of this Court in Baijnath Ked ia vs State of Bihar & Ors.,;, applied.

The appellant was the owner of a quarry in the State of Madras. He applied to the Collector for confirmation of his lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949. The Collector rejected the application on the ground that he had not been given notice of the date of expiry of the lease and that the lessee had no right to continue in possession. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order made by the Board of Revenue. Held: (i) The appellant's contention that the lease was for a period exceeding one year is not correct. The second proviso to section 20 (1) of the Abolition Act provides that if the lessee has entered into an agreement with the Government of India or any other person interested in the land, it shall be deemed to have been so terminated. The third proviso imposes a duty upon the Government to take over possession of the's late quar ries from the appellant. The words " such right " in the first proviso are wide enough to include all contracts which may be enforceable against the Government. That is to say, the Government can terminate the lease at its option and unconditionally make an award. But this is not the correct approach to the problem. If the third proviso is construed as conferring a power on the Government, it must be read along with the words " before the expiration of the term of the contract ". In other words, the word " such " in section 20 of the Amendment Act should be interpreted as referring to different subjects. Then again, there is nothing corresponding to it in the second proviso.
